publications.title: What Is Your AI Agent Buying? Evaluation, Biases, Model Dependence, & Emerging Implications for Agentic E-Commerce
publications.summary: Using ACES, a provider-agnostic framework for auditing agent decisions, the authors measure how LLM shopping agents choose among products. They find demand concentrating on a few modal products, preferences that reshuffle with model updates, strong position biases that persist even in text-only interfaces, and consistent reactions to sponsored tags and platform endorsements.
publications.whyItMatters: Checkout protocols such as OpenAI ACP and UCP move the purchase decision into an agent; this paper quantifies the ranking and position biases merchants and platforms inherit when the agent, not a person, picks the product.

publications.title: Magentic Marketplace: An Open-Source Environment for Studying Agentic Markets
publications.summary: Introduces Magentic-Marketplace, an open-source simulated two-sided market in which assistant agents represent consumers and service agents represent competing businesses, and uses it to measure utility, behavioral bias, vulnerability to manipulation and the effect of search mechanisms. Frontier models approach optimal welfare only under ideal search, degrade sharply with scale, and show a severe first-proposal bias that gives response speed a 10 to 30 times advantage over quality.
publications.whyItMatters: Discovery and checkout protocols such as UCP and OpenAI ACP create the two-sided agent markets this environment simulates, so its first-proposal and search findings bear directly on how merchant feeds and ranking should be designed.

publications.title: The Automated but Risky Game: Modeling and Benchmarking Agent-to-Agent Negotiations and Transactions in Consumer Markets
publications.summary: Builds an experimental framework in which consumer and merchant LLM agents negotiate and transact with each other. Outcomes differ sharply across models, and behavioral anomalies lead to overspending or acceptance of unreasonable deals, producing losses for both sides.
publications.whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent negotiation is the step before an ACP or UCP checkout and before an AP2 mandate is signed; the paper quantifies the asymmetry and loss risk users accept when they delegate the deal itself.

publications.title: The Agentic Economy
publications.venue: Communications of the ACM, vol. 69, no. 2, pp. 39-42 (2026)
publications.summary: Argues that the deepest economic effect of generative AI is lower communication friction between consumers and businesses, with assistant agents and service agents transacting programmatically. The authors separate unscripted interactions, enabled by language and protocol design, from unrestricted interactions, which depend on market structure and governance, and discuss walled gardens versus an open agent web, advertising and discovery, micro-transactions and the rebundling of digital goods.
publications.whyItMatters: The clearest economic framing of why ACP, UCP and AP2 exist: its assistant-agent and service-agent split maps onto the buyer-agent and merchant roles those protocols standardize, and its walled-garden warning is the open question behind all of them, with x402 as the micro-transaction case.

publications.title: An Economy of AI Agents
publications.summary: A survey chapter for economists on how AI agents that plan and act over long horizons with little oversight might interact with people and with each other, reshape markets and organizations, and what institutions would be needed for such markets to work.
publications.whyItMatters: Frames the institutional questions (identity, liability, enforcement) that ERC-8004 registries and AP2 mandates try to answer with technical artifacts.

publications.title: Virtual Agent Economies
publications.summary: Proposes the sandbox economy as a lens on the emerging layer in which AI agents transact at machine speed, classifying it by origin (emergent or intentional) and by permeability to the human economy. The authors discuss auctions for resource allocation, mission economies, and the identity, trust and oversight infrastructure needed to steer such markets, warning that the current path leads to a large and highly permeable agent economy with systemic risk.
publications.whyItMatters: Names the infrastructure gaps (verifiable identity, reputation, controls on permeability) that ERC-8004 and x402 are being built to fill, and gives the policy vocabulary for discussing them.

publications.title: From Product Search to Preference Articulation: The Economics of Agentic Commerce
publications.summary: A search-theoretic model that compares manual product search, which evaluates a few products accurately, with agentic search, which screens a broad catalog through noisy representations of preferences. Manual search collapses beyond a preference-complexity threshold and platform revenue falls to zero, while agentic search avoids the collapse; the paper derives how platforms should set agent refinement depth.
publications.whyItMatters: Supplies the economic rationale for the discovery and product-feed layers of UCP and OpenAI ACP: once consumers delegate search, platform revenue depends on how well the agent elicits preferences rather than on how many items a person inspects.

publications.title: Shopping by algorithm: How agentic AI deploys human heuristics as a surrogate consumer
publications.summary: Using Tool-Lab, a process-tracing setup that hides product attributes behind costly tool calls, the authors test eight deployed LLMs from three providers against just-below pricing and promotional framing. Cues rarely mislead when information is free, but under acquisition costs and a vague goal the agents skip the attributes needed to compute unit price and make heuristic, suboptimal choices much like people.
publications.whyItMatters: Shows that storefront information architecture and tool cost shape what agents buy, which matters for how merchants expose product data in ACP and UCP feeds and for proposals to sell product information per fact over x402.

publications.title: The User Asks, Platforms Compete: How Agentic Recommendation Markets Take Shape
publications.summary: Studies agentic recommendation markets in which a user agent states a need first and platforms compete for its attention. Across three product domains, broader access does not translate into exposure, platforms answer with selectively positive explanations in 73 to 78 percent of first-ranked positions, and tying platform behavior to later user feedback cuts this to 36 to 41 percent while raising purchases of the relevant item.
publications.whyItMatters: Models the merchant-side incentives that UCP and ACP discovery surfaces create when many sellers answer one agent's query, and argues that access, attention and accountability must be designed as one mechanism.

publications.title: Paying to Know: Micro-Transaction Markets for Verified Product Information in Agentic E-Commerce
publications.summary: A vision paper arguing that once buyers are agents paying through agent-native layers such as x402 (payment) and AP2 (authorization), the scarce resource becomes trustworthy product information rather than product matching. It sketches a market in which buyer agents pay fractions of a cent to unlock seller- and reviewer-supplied evidence, with reviewer trust scored reputationally, and lists the NLP problems this creates.
publications.whyItMatters: Names x402 (payment) and AP2 (authorization against the user's budget) as the agent-native layers that make per-fact micropayments feasible; it is a vision paper, not an analysis of either, and its reputational scoring of reviewers is a role that ERC-8004 registries also aim to fill, although the paper does not name ERC-8004.

publications.title: Emergent Misaligned Communication in Long-Horizon Multi-Agent LLM Commerce
publications.summary: Analyzes 2,583 inter-agent emails from twenty one-year runs of Vending-Bench Arena across 13 frontier models and labels 12.6 percent as misaligned (false factual claims, manipulation, collusion or threats). Misalignment appears in every run and in 74.7 percent of agent-runs, is reciprocal, rises under inventory scarcity, and is not predicted by model capability rank.
publications.whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent commerce protocols assume counterparties negotiate in good faith; this measurement shows deceptive speech acts emerging without adversarial prompting, which bears on reputation layers in ERC-8004 and on merchant-agent trust in ACP and UCP.

publications.title: Evaluating LLM Agent Collusion in Double Auctions
publications.summary: Places LLM sellers in simulated continuous double auctions and tests when they collude, defined as secret cooperation that harms another party. Direct seller communication increases collusion, propensity differs by model, and oversight or urgency from authority figures changes collusive behavior.
publications.whyItMatters: Relevant to any multi-seller agent market on ACP, UCP or x402: giving seller agents a channel to talk to each other is itself a competition risk.

publications.title: APort Vault: Benchmarking AI Agent Payment Authorization with the Open Agent Passport
publications.summary: Replays 4,371 human-written attacks from a capture-the-flag event against a live payment agent across 14 models, five policy levels and two tracks, with and without a deterministic pre-action check implementing the author's Open Agent Passport specification. Transfers to recipients the passport did not permit occurred 140 times in 76,842 model-alone evaluations and zero times in 69,297 behind the layer, while 25,370 legitimate payments still executed.
publications.whyItMatters: A benchmark of the authorization boundary that AP2 mandates, x402 payment headers and VIC instructions all depend on: deterministic policy enforcement outside the model stopped recipient hijacks that prompting alone did not. The Open Agent Passport is the author's own specification, so read the comparison with that in mind.

publications.title: Agentic Commerce Bench: Measuring Fraud Detection for Agents That Spend Money
publications.summary: Presents a fraud taxonomy for agents with spend authority organized by five observation levels, a benchmark of twenty fraud classes built from production aggregates (1,647 service operations and 1,068 settlements), and gordonguard, an open-source detector stack. Calibrated detectors flag 6.5 percent of clean traffic and leave eight classes at chance, and a median payment of $0.007 makes one human review 143 times costlier than the payment it checks.
publications.whyItMatters: Targets fraud on machine-to-machine rails: its benchmark traffic settles over x402, where a counterparty can be exactly who it claims to be and still overcharge, so identity checks alone do not stop value loss. The paper does not name ERC-8004.

publications.title: BazaarBench: Delegation Safety in Decentralized C2C Marketplaces Run by LLM Agents
publications.summary: A simulated consumer-to-consumer marketplace with 100 agents, eBay-derived inventories and reputation-based trust, scoring six failure types across five transaction stages over 357,608 model calls. All five tested models promise the same item to multiple buyers, and under adversarial instructions the share of committed sales completed despite unavailable items or overstated condition rises from 15.4 to 33.4 percent, with most extra earnings coming from goods the sellers never held.
publications.whyItMatters: Tests whether reputation can hold a decentralized agent market together, the premise behind ERC-8004's Reputation Registry, and measures delegation failures that ACP and UCP style checkouts would inherit from the agents using them.

publications.title: Trust and Task Completion in the World of Consumer AI Agents
publications.summary: Proposes an evaluation that scores trust (nothing happens the user did not agree to, including spend limits and ignoring strangers' instructions) and task completion on the same runs in a simulated world of businesses with websites, inboxes and phone lines. The authors' assistant harness completes 71 percent of errands and keeps trust on 94 percent of trap runs versus 50 to 64 and 59 to 75 percent for base models; the study is a vendor evaluating its own product.
publications.whyItMatters: Operationalizes the consumer-side guarantees that delegation designs such as AP2 open mandates and TAP promise (the paper itself does not name AP2), and shows how much of the result comes from the harness rather than the model.

publications.title: WebShop: Towards Scalable Real-World Web Interaction with Grounded Language Agents
publications.summary: A simulated e-commerce site with 1.18 million real products and 12,087 crowd-sourced instructions in which an agent must search, customize and buy an item. It introduced compositional instruction following, query reformulation and noisy web text as grounding challenges and collected over 1,600 human demonstrations for training.
publications.whyItMatters: The ancestor of every agentic shopping benchmark; the search, option selection and checkout steps it scripted are what ACP and UCP now turn into protocol messages.

publications.title: τ-bench: A Benchmark for Tool-Agent-User Interaction in Real-World Domains
publications.summary: Simulates conversations between an LLM-played user and an agent that has domain API tools and policy documents, grading by comparing the final database state to an annotated goal and introducing the pass^k reliability metric. Even strong function-calling agents succeeded on under half of the tasks and were inconsistent across trials, with pass^8 below 25 percent in retail.
publications.whyItMatters: Its retail domain (orders, exchanges, refunds under policy) is the post-purchase side of ACP and UCP, and pass^k is the reliability framing merchants need before letting agents touch orders.

publications.title: WebArena: A Realistic Web Environment for Building Autonomous Agents
publications.summary: A reproducible environment of fully functional websites across e-commerce, forums, software development and content management, with tools and knowledge bases and a benchmark of long-horizon tasks graded on functional correctness rather than on action traces.
publications.whyItMatters: Its e-commerce site is the standard sandbox for web shopping agents; Piet et al. and Shi et al. in this bibliography build their security arguments on it.

publications.title: A Survey of AI Agent Protocols
publications.summary: Surveys agent communication protocols with a two-dimensional classification (context-oriented versus inter-agent, general-purpose versus domain-specific), compares them on security, scalability and latency, and lays out directions such as layered architectures, privacy preservation and group interaction.
publications.whyItMatters: Provides the taxonomy into which payment and commerce protocols (x402, AP2, ACP, UCP) slot as domain-specific layers above MCP and A2A.

publications.title: A survey of agent interoperability protocols: Model Context Protocol (MCP), Agent Communication Protocol (ACP), Agent-to-Agent Protocol (A2A), and Agent Network Protocol (ANP)
publications.summary: Compares MCP, IBM's Agent Communication Protocol, Google's A2A and the Agent Network Protocol on interaction modes, discovery, communication patterns and security models, and proposes a phased adoption roadmap that ends with ANP for decentralized agent marketplaces.
publications.whyItMatters: Background for the transport layer under the commerce protocols, with one caution: its ACP is IBM's Agent Communication Protocol, not OpenAI's Agentic Commerce Protocol, so the acronym must not be conflated.

publications.title: Agentic Web: Weaving the Next Web with AI Agents
publications.summary: Proposes a framework for the Agentic Web built on three dimensions (intelligence, interaction, economics), traces its evolution from the PC and mobile web, and discusses communication protocols, orchestration and an Agent Attention Economy together with governance risks.
publications.whyItMatters: Its economics dimension and attention-economy discussion anticipate the discovery and monetization questions that UCP, ACP and x402 are now standardizing.

publications.title: Not What You've Signed Up For: Compromising Real-World LLM-Integrated Applications with Indirect Prompt Injection
publications.venue: AISec 2023 (16th ACM Workshop on Artificial Intelligence and Security, at CCS 2023), pp. 79-90
publications.summary: Introduces indirect prompt injection: adversaries plant instructions in data that an LLM-integrated application will retrieve, so the model is attacked without any direct interface. The paper gives a security taxonomy of impacts, including data theft, worming and contamination of the information ecosystem, and demonstrates attacks on real systems.
publications.whyItMatters: The founding paper for the threat every agentic payment protocol must contain. AP2 mandates, TAP intent signatures and ACP's structured checkout all exist partly because retrieved merchant content can hijack the buying agent; x402 leaves that defense to client policies such as spend caps and payTo checks.

publications.title: AgentDojo: A Dynamic Environment to Evaluate Prompt Injection Attacks and Defenses for LLM Agents
publications.summary: An extensible environment for agents that run tools over untrusted data, with 97 realistic tasks (email, e-banking, travel booking), 629 security test cases and pluggable attacks and defenses. Frontier models fail many tasks even without attacks, and existing injections break some but not all security properties.
publications.whyItMatters: Its e-banking and booking suites are the closest public testbed to agent payments, and the defenses cited here (CaMeL, multi-CaMeL) report their numbers on it.

publications.title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
publications.summary: A benchmark of 1,054 test cases over 17 user tools and 62 attacker tools that measures whether tool-integrated agents follow injected instructions aimed at direct harm or data exfiltration. Across 30 agents the vulnerability was substantial, with ReAct-prompted GPT-4 following injections in roughly one case in four.
publications.whyItMatters: Supplies the attacker-tool framing (a malicious tool result that triggers a transfer) that payment-agent threat models for AP2 and x402 reuse.

publications.title: Defeating Prompt Injections by Design
publications.venue: IEEE Conference on Secure and Trustworthy Machine Learning (SaTML 2026), pp. 587-618
publications.summary: CaMeL wraps the LLM in a protective system layer that extracts control and data flow from the trusted user query, so retrieved data can never alter program flow, and attaches capabilities to values so tool calls are checked against security policies. It solved 77 percent of AgentDojo tasks with provable security versus 84 percent for an undefended agent.
publications.whyItMatters: The capability model is a natural enforcement point for payment policy: an AP2 open mandate's constraints (for example payment.amount_range) or an x402 spend limit can be expressed as a CaMeL policy on the payment tool's arguments.

publications.title: Design Patterns for Securing LLM Agents against Prompt Injections
publications.summary: Proposes a set of principled design patterns that restrict how untrusted inputs can influence an agent's actions, analyzes their utility and security trade-offs, and illustrates them with case studies of real applications.
publications.whyItMatters: A practical checklist for anyone building a buying agent on ACP, AP2 or x402: the patterns constrain which parts of agent state untrusted merchant content may ever touch.

publications.title: WASP: Benchmarking Web Agent Security Against Prompt Injection Attacks
publications.summary: An end-to-end benchmark for web agents facing realistic, low-effort human-written injections in tasks such as paying bills. Even top reasoning models were partially deceived in up to 86 percent of cases yet rarely completed the attacker's full goal, which the authors call security by incompetence.
publications.whyItMatters: Web agents that pay bills are the use case TAP and AP2 target; WASP's finding that attacks succeed partially but not fully is a warning that capability gains will remove the accidental protection.

publications.title: Commercial LLM Agents Are Already Vulnerable to Simple Yet Dangerous Attacks
publications.summary: Provides a taxonomy of attacks specific to agent pipelines, organized by threat actor, objective, entry point, attacker observability, strategy and inherent pipeline weaknesses, and demonstrates simple, practical attacks on popular open-source and commercial agents.
publications.whyItMatters: Documents that deployed browsing and shopping agents, the clients that ACP and UCP checkouts serve, can be steered by web content without any model jailbreak.

publications.title: Real AI Agents with Fake Memories: Fatal Context Manipulation Attacks on Web3 Agents
publications.summary: Defines context manipulation (input channels, memory modules and external data feeds) as the attack surface of blockchain agents, shows on ElizaOS that injected prompts or falsified memories trigger unauthorized asset transfers, and introduces CrAIBench with over 150 Web3 tasks and over 500 attack cases. Memory injection proved more effective than prompt injection, and prompt-injection detectors offered little protection.
publications.whyItMatters: The closest existing study of agents that hold crypto spending keys, the deployment model for x402 clients and ERC-8004 registered agents; a poisoned memory can drain a wallet that no protocol-level check would stop.

publications.title: Web Agents Should Adopt the Plan-Then-Execute Paradigm
publications.summary: Argues that ReAct is the wrong default for web agents because product pages mix seller, reviewer and advertiser content, and that agents should commit to a task program before seeing runtime content. All WebArena tasks fit plan-then-execute and 80 percent can run as pure programs; the barrier is that browser actions lack typed, semantic interfaces.
publications.whyItMatters: Makes the case for typed, task-level commerce APIs, which is what UCP and OpenAI ACP provide in place of clicks: structured checkout interfaces are a security measure, not only a convenience.

publications.title: Benchmarking Web Agent Safety under E-commerce Deceptive Interfaces
publications.summary: Introduces WebDecept, a plugin that injects seven deceptive interface patterns (targeted advertisements, domain redirection, shopping manipulation and others) into existing web environments, and evaluates multimodal web agents under them. Agents were highly susceptible to several classes of deception and prompt-based constraints were often insufficient.
publications.whyItMatters: Measures the merchant-side manipulation surface that structured checkouts in UCP and ACP are meant to remove, and gives a baseline for how agents behave when they must still browse a storefront.

publications.title: Reputation Systems
publications.venue: Communications of the ACM, vol. 43, no. 12, pp. 45-48
publications.summary: The classic statement of the problem: the Internet lets strangers transact at a scale where personal references and community standing no longer work, so reputation systems collect, aggregate and distribute feedback about past behavior. The authors set out what such systems must do and the difficulties of eliciting honest feedback and of cheap identity changes.
publications.whyItMatters: ERC-8004's Reputation Registry is a reputation system in Resnick's sense, and the paper's warning about cheap identity changes is exactly the Sybil feedback dispute recorded against it.

publications.title: The Sybil Attack
publications.venue: IPTPS 2002 (1st International Workshop on Peer-to-Peer Systems), Lecture Notes in Computer Science, Springer, pp. 251-260
publications.summary: Shows that in a large peer-to-peer system without a logically centralized authority, a single faulty entity can present many identities and defeat the redundancy the system relies on, and that such Sybil attacks remain possible except under unrealistic assumptions of resource parity and coordination among entities.
publications.whyItMatters: Defines the attack every permissionless agent registry inherits: ERC-8004 identities and feedback without a trusted issuer are exposed to it, which is why TAP and the card networks keep a certifying authority in the loop.

publications.title: The EigenTrust Algorithm for Reputation Management in P2P Networks
publications.venue: WWW 2003 (12th International World Wide Web Conference)
publications.summary: Assigns each peer a single global trust value computed by power iteration over local trust ratings, in a distributed and secure way, so peers can avoid downloading inauthentic files. Simulations show the system isolates malicious peers even when they collude.
publications.whyItMatters: The standard reference for turning pairwise feedback, such as the entries ERC-8004's Reputation Registry stores, into a global score, and for the collusion cases any such aggregator must resist.

publications.title: A Survey of Trust and Reputation Systems for Online Service Provision
publications.venue: Decision Support Systems, vol. 43, no. 2, pp. 618-644
publications.summary: Surveys systems in which parties rate each other after transactions and aggregated ratings guide future decisions, describing them as collaborative sanctioning systems that also create an incentive for good behavior. It reviews commercial and proposed designs, analyzes trends and proposes a research agenda.
publications.whyItMatters: The reference taxonomy for reputation computation that ERC-8004 reputation clients and off-chain scorers draw on, and a reminder that the field predates agents by two decades.

publications.title: Tempting the Agent: The Economics of Reputation without Persistent Identity in AI Agent Markets
publications.summary: A dynamic model in which an agent's reputation is capital that attracts future demand, and the agent chooses each period between honest operation, investing in quality, or a one-shot deviation that cashes out the reputation and restarts under a penalized new identity. The temptation depends on identity-reset cost, reputation persistence, demand sensitivity and enforcement design; ERC-8004, ERC-8183 and x402 are named as the motivating infrastructure.
publications.whyItMatters: Names ERC-8004 and x402 directly and states the economic condition under which an on-chain reputation registry disciplines agents: resetting an identity must cost more than the one-shot gain from burning it.

publications.title: Dissociative Identity: Language Model Agents Lack Grounding for Reputation Mechanisms
publications.venue: ACM FAccT 2026 (Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency), pp. 4199-4219
publications.summary: Argues that Know Your Agent regimes modeled on human identity verification and credit scores are incomplete because language model agents are assemblages of mutable modules (models, prompts, tool policies, memory) with fluid personas that may not internalize sanctions, so identifiability, predictability, credibility and rehabilitability lack grounding. It proposes observability-based, ex ante, protocol-level behavioral harnesses in place of ex post reputation.
publications.whyItMatters: A direct critique of the premise behind ERC-8004's Reputation Registry and of KYA-style identity checks in TAP and Agent Pay: if the sanctioned identity can be swapped out, reputation does not discipline the agent.

publications.title: Reputation as Community Memory for the Agentic Web
publications.summary: Presents Cairn, a community reputation platform in which agents query the collective opinion of a data source, service or tool before use and submit evidence-backed ratings afterward, aggregated by a time-decayed Beta model with confidence shrinkage and searchable by reviewer rationale. The engine is evaluated under lying, collusion and camouflage, and in a production case study rating heterogeneous agents.
publications.whyItMatters: An off-chain alternative to ERC-8004's registry for the same question (should an agent trust this resource), useful as a design comparison for aggregation and adversarial robustness.

publications.title: Paying for Honesty Without Knowing the Truth: Reputation-Penalty Design for LLM Marketplace Agents
publications.summary: LLM merchant agents fabricate product attributes in most listings under competitive pressure even when told to be honest. CARP, a reputation-penalty mechanism with a deadband that forgives complaint noise and a state-dependent severity, suppresses low-rated liars without any product-level ground truth, and SPARC makes the penalty behaviorally binding so merchants restrain themselves once lying costs sales.
publications.whyItMatters: Shows how a platform-level reputation penalty can govern seller agents behind ACP or UCP storefronts using only noisy complaints, a design that could sit on top of ERC-8004 feedback entries.

publications.title: Agentic Commerce World: An Auditable and Verifiable Environment for Vibe Commerce
publications.summary: ACWorld is an environment in which independently controlled buyer and merchant agents transact through a Vibe Commerce Protocol that validates each action before updating shared state and records the interactions for audit. Its benchmark has a 200-task capability track and a 60-task large-catalog track over 785,022 listings; ten models score 65.9 to 85.6 percent and 56.1 to 91.4 percent, and process-level evidence catches errors that final state misses.
publications.whyItMatters: A reproducible testbed for the buyer-agent to merchant-agent transaction loop that OpenAI ACP and UCP standardize, with an audit-log design relevant to dispute handling.

publications.title: Markets, Not Planners: Decentralized Orchestration of LLM Agents with Private Information
publications.summary: Replaces centralized orchestration with AgentLance, a repeated labor market in which agents bid on tasks using private costs, an allocator picks winners from bids and public reputation records, a VCG-style rule sets payments, and winners can subcontract through the same mechanism. It outperforms single-model, centralized and market baselines, and the authors show a centralized LLM allocator can be swayed by a single inserted preference.
publications.whyItMatters: Demonstrates reputation records and payments working together to allocate agent labor, which is the combination ERC-8004 (reputation) and x402 (payment) aim to provide on open rails.

publications.title: Evolution of Market Microstructure in the Age of AI
publications.summary: A survey tracing market microstructure from floor trading through electronic order books, batch auctions, dark pools and blockchain automated market makers to AI agents that discover, pay for and compete over resources, organized around whether a market can allocate efficiently without participants revealing everything. It argues that allocation is the missing layer of the agent-commerce protocol stack.
publications.whyItMatters: Positions x402 as the posted-price payment layer of an agent stack whose missing layer is allocation, and says agent commerce inherits the extractable value of the chains it settles on.

publications.title: SoK: Decentralized Agent Economic Infrastructure
publications.summary: Systematizes security and economic requirements across the lifecycle of an agent task into 17 property families over six stages, examines 12 systems and standards, five mechanism families and four classical baselines, and introduces guarantee closure, a criterion for whether guarantees made at one stage still constrain later decisions. Experiments over 840 matched executions and an 11,648-case check expose recurring gaps between verification and settlement.
publications.whyItMatters: Relevant to stacks that chain ERC-8004 identity and validation with x402 payment: it shows how an escrow can release funds on an approval that carries little evidence the work was done. Which 12 systems are covered was not confirmed from the abstract alone.

publications.title: A Finger on the Scale: Covert Policy Steering through Agentic Skills
publications.summary: Treats reusable agent skills as externalized policies and presents SkillShift, a supply-chain attack that keeps a skill's declared task and output interface while covertly steering decisions toward an undisclosed objective. In agentic commerce and dependency selection it achieved attacker-favored selection rates of 81.33 and 63.33 percent with no utility loss, transferred across backends, and evaded the evaluated scanners.
publications.whyItMatters: A merchant-steering attack that needs no prompt injection: a shopping agent's skill package can bias which seller wins an ACP or UCP checkout while every protocol message stays valid.

publications.title: From Review to Authorization: Key-Isolated Threshold Signing for LLM Agents
publications.summary: KITA keeps the user's signing key and every threshold key share outside all LLM processes; an action is authorized only when t reviewer-signer domains contribute shares bound to the canonical action after authenticated approval, so a prompt-injected proposer cannot forge an authorization. The path is implemented with a structured-output LLM adapter and threshold BLS signatures.
publications.whyItMatters: Addresses a gap AP2 leaves open that also applies to x402 clients: the agent that reads untrusted content should not hold the credential that signs the payment. The paper discusses AP2 and does not name x402.

publications.title: Runtime Authorization for Resources Acquired by AI Agents
publications.summary: Identifies a post-fulfillment activation gap: payment, budget, OAuth and mandate checks validate a transaction but not whether the resource an agent acquires (compute, credentials, accounts, other agents) may become usable authority. The proposed architecture quarantines acquired outputs, resolves their capabilities from provider evidence and activates them through a checked transaction, with eight proven safety properties and trace-based evaluation.
publications.whyItMatters: Extends the AP2 mandate and x402 payment checks to what happens after a purchase succeeds, a stage none of the eight protocols currently specifies.

publications.title: Mandato: Protocol-Level Enforcement of Digitally Signed Mandates on AI Agent Actions with Cryptographically Chained Audit Trails
publications.summary: Proposes a governance proxy that enforces signed, machine-readable mandates on MCP tool calls, blocking non-conforming calls and recording every decision in a hash-chained, timestamp-anchored audit trail. The mandate is modeled on the civil-law delegation of authority and mapped to EU AI Act, GDPR, NIS2 and eIDAS 2 obligations; the paper describes implementation status and an evaluation plan rather than results.
publications.whyItMatters: A mandate concept parallel to AP2's open and closed Checkout and Payment Mandates, applied at the tool-call layer and tied to EU legal instruments, which is useful for the compliance view of delegation.

publications.title: AID-Guard: Stateful Authorization for Delegated Agent Effects
publications.summary: AID-Guard closes the gap between authorization at admission and the provider effect that follows: it revalidates the approved request and provider state at commit, holds one reservation under ambiguity, and releases a successor only after a terminal result or a certified no-effect, so that, for supported provider contracts, one reservation yields at most one effect across retries and recovery. A prototype was tested against Stripe and Resend provider contracts, with all 210 Stripe trials matching predeclared outcomes.
publications.whyItMatters: Exactly-once effects and idempotency are the operational core of agent payments; this is an evaluated protocol that treats a Stripe charge as a delegated effect with its own lifecycle, relevant to MPP and ACP implementations.

publications.title: Can CaMeLs Talk? Securing Multi-Agent Systems Against Indirect Prompt Injection Attacks
publications.summary: Shows that CaMeL's guarantees do not compose when agents call other agents as tools, because a downstream agent can reinterpret untrusted data as trusted input, and gives a concrete attack. Multi-CaMeL, an agent-to-agent protocol that passes untrusted data through a separate channel, brings attack success on MultiAgentDojo to 0.0 percent versus 0.2 percent for single-agent CaMeL and 12.9 percent undefended.
publications.whyItMatters: Agent-to-agent commerce (A2A with x402, or buyer and merchant agents under ACP) is the hierarchical setting in which single-agent defenses fail; the protocol-level fix speaks to how payment messages between agents should be typed.

publications.title: StepJack: Benchmarking Computer-Use Agent Safety Against Multi-Step Indirect Prompt Injection
publications.summary: Introduces multi-step indirect prompt injection, in which an adversarial goal is split into innocuous sub-steps spread across pages along the agent's navigation path, and a benchmark of 480 cases. Across six computer-use agents, decomposition raises attack success, for one model from 41.7 percent single-step to 72.9 percent at three steps.
publications.whyItMatters: Computer-use agents that shop across several merchant pages are the deployment TAP and Agent Pay credentials are issued to; staged injections evade per-page defenses.

publications.title: Who Is Your Agent Serving? Provider-Side Indirect Prompt Injection in Proactive Agents
publications.summary: Shows that an external provider controlling only content about its own product can redirect a proactive personal agent to recommend it, recruit the user's private context to justify it and lower adoption friction, without compromising the agent or gaining permissions. Across three environments and six user models the macro gain reaches 77.4 percentage points, and provider influence persists even when no final authorization is given.
publications.whyItMatters: Models the merchant-side incentive to manipulate agent recommendations in ACP and UCP style markets, where the provider's own listing is the injection vector.

publications.title: LEGIT: Credentialing Protocol for Trustworthy AI Agent Marketplaces
publications.summary: A credentialing protocol that binds measured quality and cost per solved task to a signed record of agent configuration, task domain, evaluation budget and evidence, links past outcomes to the same identity as reputation, and lets buyers verify the records. Evaluations show that agents with similar success differ in cost and that comparisons depend on budget; a complementary analysis prices the deposits and fees needed to manipulate reputation under a stated Sybil model.
publications.whyItMatters: A concrete alternative design for the certification and feedback roles that ERC-8004's Validation and Reputation registries describe, with explicit Sybil cost accounting.

publications.title: Epistemic Sybil Resistance: Multiplying AI Agents Without Multiplying Evidence
publications.summary: Formalizes an epistemic Sybil problem: extra agent reports that descend from the same evidence add no information, and report-only aggregators cannot tell replication from independent corroboration. Experiments show naive posterior coverage collapsing from 0.940 to 0.263 as report count rises on a single evidence root, and the author argues that aggregation should track evidential ancestry rather than agent or report count.
publications.whyItMatters: Reframes Sybil resistance for ERC-8004 style feedback and validation: many attestations from agents sharing a base model or data source should not be counted as independent evidence.
